nodes.text: INSTANT · ON-DEVICE AI The document outlines the United States Constitution, specifically the Articles of Confederation (p.1–4). It establishes that the executive power is vested in a President elected by electors from states (p.5), while the legislative body includes two Houses: the House of Representatives chosen by state legislatures and one Senate. Both houses must pass bills to be enacted, with the Senate requiring two-thirds vote prior to becoming law; no single house can override a defeated bill without unanimous consent. The Constitution grants specific powers such as regulating commerce, establishing banks, coinage, weights/measurements, tax collection, raising armies, maintaining a navy, and governing them (p.2–3). It also restricts state actions by prohibiting states from making laws impairing contracts or granting titles of nobility without Congressional consent (p.4), and ensures that no new state can be formed by joining other states. Crimes including treason require two witnesses or confession in open court to meet the standard for conviction, not just one witness (p.5). No person convicted of treason may be deprived of property except with Congress's consent (p.6). Continuing from where the text stops: 3. No State may lay duties or taxes on imports or exports without Congressional consent, except for necessary expenses. • 4. A Quorum for choosing the President consists of two-thirds of the States' Representatives; a majority is required to choose the President directly. Summary of all 9 pages.
